title: Return Stacking Explained - Open Interest - Ep.16

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Return Stacking Explained - Open Interest - Ep.16.docx

speakers: Adam Butler (Resolve Asset Management / Return Stacked)
summary: Open Interest ep.16 (Apr-Jun 2025): return stacking and portable alpha ETFs; top-down and bottom-up replication of the SG Trend Index; ETF capacity and liquidity; stacking limits; merger arbitrage and gold/Bitcoin overlays.

coverage.note: preview of later point (30/70 blend), intro, guest background
portable alpha and return stacking concept
ETF vs mutual fund; ETF liquidity
capacity, CFTC limits, universe size, no closing
stability of fitted weights; market set limits
rationale for blend; CTA index replication
feature families, ETFs as benchmark, crisis offset
vol levels, high-vol trend, client vol tolerance

completeness_estimate: 0.80 - first reader captured every main design point (return stacking, wrapper limits, bottom-up and top-down replication, blend, 18f-4, merger arbitrage, overlays); missed supporting reasons (blend motivation, wrapper trade-offs, dispersion sources, funded beta, fee squeeze) and mislabelled several speakers in the Cory/Adam exchange.

claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
claims.quote: how can you keep your beta in your portfolio, the core stocks and bonds that institutions are building their strategic asset allocation around, but search for alpha in more fruitful places
claims.claim: Portable alpha / return stacking keeps core stock and bond beta and uses futures, swaps and capital efficiency to free capital for other alpha sources (trend, carry, merger arb).

claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
claims.quote: struggled against the non-stop outperformance particularly here in the US of a core US6040
claims.claim: Selling alternatives by asking investors to cut stocks and bonds failed in the 2010s; a capital-efficient stacked product avoids that behavioural obstacle.
claims.conditions: strong US 60/40 period

claims.speaker: Adam Butler
claims.quote: the mutual fund strategies are able to trade a a slightly wider and more diverse group of futures markets
claims.claim: Mutual fund wrappers can trade a wider futures set than ETFs because ETF market makers need liquid hedges for creations and redemptions.

claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
claims.quote: most of the futures based products that are coming out from Alpha Simplex and ManHL and Invesco and Black Rockck tend to be subset a
claims.claim: Futures-based ETF trend products use a subset of the most liquid US and European markets versus the full set in their mutual fund and hedge fund versions.

claims.speaker: Adam Butler
claims.quote: badass spreads of 20 30 [L160] basis points on average I don't think are unusual
claims.claim: Small-size ETF trades in less liquid futures baskets face bid-ask spreads of 20-30 bp on average and wider in stress; large trades via institutional desks can be done near NAV, and holding long term smooths cost.
claims.conditions: small trade size, chaotic markets

claims.speaker: Adam Butler
claims.quote: CFTC limits that limit the number of contracts that can be held in the front month
claims.claim: CFTC limits on front-month positions can be bypassed by trading back-month contracts, giving 10x or more capacity.

claims.speaker: Adam Butler
claims.quote: you can get pretty darn close in replication space with a much more finite universe of markets as long as you're spanning the equity index, bond index, commodity, and currencies
claims.claim: A 26-27 market universe covering equities, bonds, commodities and currencies (70-80% of global futures liquidity) replicates the full CTA universe closely because all players trade in proportion to liquidity.

claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
claims.quote: you can't close the ETF. So, we have to be able to run it at in theory infinite scale.
claims.claim: An ETF cannot be closed to inflows, so the strategy must be run identically at all sizes; at extreme scale performance would degrade and self-correct.
claims.conditions: very large AUM

claims.speaker: Adam Butler
claims.quote: we regressed all of these individual market individual trend length strategies on the societ general trend index over the very long term
claims.claim: Bottom-up replication: for each market build time-series trend strategies with lookbacks from 5 to 300 days and regress them on the SG Trend Index (daily since 2000) to pick the weights that best fit.

claims.speaker: Adam Butler
claims.quote: the bottomup strategy actually does just a really good job with an average correlation daily correlation in the neighborhood of kind of 0.8
claims.claim: The bottom-up replication achieves about 0.8 daily correlation to the SG Trend Index, which is an average of 10 funds with differing styles.

claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
claims.quote: You get intermediate term trend speeds and you get 25% of your risk weight pretty much in equity indices, in bonds, in commodities, in currencies.
claims.claim: Fitting to the SG Trend Index gives intermediate trend speeds and about equal 25% risk weights in equities, bonds, commodities and currencies, with commodity risk split evenly between metals and energies.

claims.speaker: Adam Butler
claims.quote: for all the markets you're trading to have gone through meaningful periods of contributing positive or negative P&L
claims.claim: Fitting trend weights needs 15-20 years of data because a market that produced no P&L in a decade cannot be distinguished from one managers did not trade.

correction.issue: Attributed to Adam Butler. The 15-20 year training-window answer comes from Cory's reply to the recalibration question; Adam only speaks from 'We also, when we were investigating this ...' and then says 'to Corey's point'.
correction.fix: Cory: fitting trend weights needs 15-20 years of data because a market that produced no P&L in a decade cannot be told apart from one managers did not trade, so rerunning each year will not change weights meaningfully.

claims.speaker: Adam Butler
claims.quote: the sector weight was still very consistent
claims.claim: Fitted market weights change by decade (S&P trendless in 2000-10, trendy 2010-20) but sector weights and trend speeds stay stable under cross-validation, and there is no evidence that trend length rose systematically 2000-2020.

claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
claims.quote: as you grow in AUM the less liquid markets that you trade end up having a smaller impact on total portfolio P&L
claims.claim: The trend index consists of the largest managers, whose less liquid markets matter little to P&L, so a limited-market replication tracks them well.

claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
claims.quote: coffee was a big one, uh, in 2024, uh, and 2023
claims.claim: Idiosyncratic bets such as coffee in 2023-24 created manager dispersion that later reversed, and on average dispersion balances out.

claims.speaker: Adam Butler
claims.quote: 80% of their risk weights probably in the same 20 markets we could all rattle off the top of our head
claims.claim: Large trend managers put about 80% of risk in the same ~20 markets, and averaging the fat-tail weights across managers attenuates toward zero, so the beta can be captured with a handful of common markets.

correction.issue: Speaker is given as Adam, but the passage continues without a break from the speaker who gave the coffee example (C09-1, Cory); no change of speaker is shown.
correction.fix: Same speaker as C09-1 (Cory): large trend managers put about 80% of risk in the same ~20 markets; averaging the fat-tail weights across managers attenuates toward zero, so the beta can be captured with a handful of common markets.

claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
claims.quote: is a regressionbased approach, right? Where we're going to look at the most recent performance of something like the sock gen trend index
claims.claim: Top-down replication: run a robust regression of recent index returns on futures markets to find the long/short basket that mimics it, assuming weights hold one day ahead.
claims.indicator: robust regression of SG Trend Index on futures

claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
claims.quote: it can capture the return of markets that we're not necessarily trading because of the way regression works
claims.claim: Top-down regression is flexible and can approximate untraded markets (e.g. Swiss franc via gold and euro) and capture manager innovation.

claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
claims.quote: it is by definition rearward facing
claims.claim: Top-down weights lag by the 20-40 day lookback (regional bank crisis 2023 shift missed) and cannot see positions in markets with no recent P&L.
claims.conditions: after sudden manager repositioning, flat markets

claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
claims.quote: the two systems are almost identical, they're statistically indistinguishable
claims.claim: Top-down and bottom-up replicate the trend index equally well, but their tracking errors are weakly correlated, so a 30% top-down / 70% bottom-up blend lowers tracking error.
claims.indicator: blend of top-down and bottom-up replication

claims.speaker: Adam Butler
claims.quote: the top down is an expression of epistemological humility
claims.claim: Top-down is kept because managers constantly innovate; it captures idiosyncratic methods the continuous bottom-up misses, even though bottom-up has better average fit.

claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
claims.quote: I'll say it makes it harder to do the bottom up for sure.
claims.claim: Replicating the broader CTA index (with mean reversion, VIX trading, carry) is harder bottom-up; Andrew Beer's CTA fund uses only top-down.

claims.speaker: Adam Butler
claims.quote: They improve the explanatory fit against the CTA index to a larger extent than they improve it relative to the trend index
claims.claim: Adding carry, skewness, seasonality and relative-value features improves fit to the CTA index much more than to the trend index, where the gain is marginal.

claims.speaker: Moritz (co-host)
claims.quote: you better beat these ETFs who replicate, as you say, or who give access, costefficient access to the beta of our industry
claims.claim: Replication ETFs form a cheap benchmark that performance-fee hedge funds must beat over the long run.

claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
claims.quote: because you're putting so much of your risk budget in this longer tale of markets, you don't necessarily get the same crisis offset
claims.claim: Per Quantica, a longer tail of markets raises Sharpe but diverts risk from markets tied to big macro factors, reducing crisis offset.

claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
claims.quote: those hedge funds that are doing very generic trend, uh, I think you're right, are just going to get squeezed out by lower cost
claims.claim: Generic trend beta is available in QIS at 10-15 bp, so managers must differentiate through spreads, breakout, speed, or fat-tail markets.

claims.speaker: Moritz (co-host)
claims.quote: most of the funds in our space have lowered their volatility profiles in recent years
claims.claim: Trend funds now run 8-12% volatility, so returns lack the punch of 1980s-90s CTAs, trading off stress payoff.

claims.speaker: Adam Butler
claims.quote: a very high ball [L520] trend strategy
claims.claim: A high-vol trend strategy is a capital-efficient version of a low-vol one (50 vol with a fifth of capital equals 10 vol) and at the limit a portable alpha overlay.

correction.issue: Attributed to Adam, but the co-host next responds 'to what Corey just said about the blowout risk' and 'I agree with you, Cory', so the passage is Cory's.
correction.fix: Cory: a high-volatility trend strategy is a capital-efficient version of a low-vol one (50 vol with a fifth of the capital equals 10 vol) and at the limit a portable alpha overlay, ignoring knock-out leverage risk.

claims.speaker: Adam Butler
claims.quote: most clients can't tolerate more than 10 ball
claims.claim: Most clients cannot tolerate more than about 10% vol and line-item risk, so products shifted to 10-12% vol.

correction.issue: Attributed to Adam, but it is the same passage by Cory (co-host replies 'I agree with you, Cory').
correction.fix: Cory (citing Cliff Asness): most clients cannot tolerate more than about 10% volatility and line-item risk is too big, so the major players moved to 10-12% vol and products with higher vol struggle.

claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
claims.quote: you would not combine things that are closely correlated
claims.claim: Stack only low-correlation components such as equity plus trend, which diversify each other.

claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
claims.quote: you can only have a 20day 99 percentile VAR of either 20% or two times your relevant benchmark
claims.claim: SEC Rule 18f-4 caps fund VaR at 20% or two times the benchmark, limiting how far stacking can be pushed.
claims.conditions: US ETFs and mutual funds

claims.speaker: Adam Butler
claims.quote: the risk of ruin is is fairly negligible and also I mean we only need at maximum kind of 25 or 30% uh of the of the total portfolio value to collateralize
claims.claim: Nightly rebalancing keeps the beta/trend ratio fixed after losses; trend collateral needs only 25-30% of NAV with 40-50% cash buffer, so ruin risk is negligible, as seen in the April 2025 drawdown.
claims.conditions: drawdown in both stocks and trend

claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
claims.quote: it typically doesn't get all the way to the buyout price
claims.claim: Merger arbitrage earns a spread equal to time value of money plus deal-break risk premium; generic strategies earned about 200-250 bp over SOFR over 20 years.

claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
claims.quote: correlation of just 0.5 to the credit risk premium
claims.claim: Merger arbitrage has low correlation to equity, bond and credit premia (about 0.5 to credit), making it a diversifying stack.

claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
claims.quote: they're using a machine learning model to look at effectively the quality of the deal
claims.claim: The Alpha Beta merger arbitrage index uses machine learning on spread, acquirer and industry to estimate deal-close probability and includes only deals that clear a return hurdle; stock-deal acquirers are hedged short or via swaps.
claims.conditions: US-listed deals above size threshold

claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
claims.quote: There's diversifying strategies and there's diversifying assets.
claims.claim: Stacked suite distinguishes diversifying strategies (trend, carry, merger) from diversifying assets (gold, Bitcoin) as overlays on equities and bonds.

claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
claims.quote: gold in particular, and I think Bitcoin is proving some of these features, uh, can be a very interesting long-term diversifier for a stock bond portfolio
claims.claim: A risk-balanced gold plus Bitcoin overlay on US equity offers a store-of-value diversifier to a stock-bond portfolio.

claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
claims.quote: has largely been out of the reach for most individuals and wealth managers who aren't going to manage a book of derivatives themselves
claims.claim: Portable alpha was an institutional tool for about 40 years and out of reach for individuals and wealth managers who will not run a derivatives book; return stacking packages it as a ticker so the capital-efficient structure can be bought without managing the derivatives.
claims.conditions: Needs a fund wrapper that runs the derivatives.

claims.speaker: Moritz (co-host)
claims.quote: a risk parity type of bond and equity allocation depending on which level volume run it on um is something like a portable alpha product at the end of the day
claims.claim: A levered risk-parity bond and equity allocation (and some QIS products) already works as a portable-alpha product, so investors may hold the concept without knowing it; return stacking makes it explicit.
claims.conditions: Depends on the volatility target and leverage used.
claims.testable: partly - risk parity exposure decomposes into stacked beta

claims.speaker: Adam Butler
claims.quote: the ETF wrapper has some tax advantages. It has the intraday liquidity. It has the ease of platform access etc.
claims.claim: Wrapper choice is a trade-off: an ETF gives tax efficiency, intraday liquidity and easy platform access, whereas a mutual fund (end-of-day NAV) can trade a wider futures set; the same strategy can run in both.
claims.direction: ETF for access, mutual fund for market breadth
claims.conditions: US tax treatment; Europe lacks the ETF tax advantage.

claims.speaker: Adam Butler
claims.quote: The market makers are always going to whenever there's less uh transparency, they're going to widen out and thin out
claims.claim: Because market makers cannot see the full basket of an active futures ETF, they widen and thin quotes, so wide spreads are a persistent feature, not a temporary one; the cost is worth it for a one-way buy-and-hold investor.
claims.indicator: ETF bid-ask spread and basket transparency
claims.conditions: Persistent when underlying markets are less liquid and traded daily.

claims.speaker: Adam Butler
claims.quote: there's a trade-off between accessibility, liquidity, and the diversity of bets that are available
claims.claim: Any fund faces a capacity trade-off: more diverse bets raise expected performance, but liquidity limits what can be traded at size, so at some point the markets you can trade no longer matter to P&L; this holds for hedge funds, mutual funds and ETFs.
claims.conditions: Binding as assets grow.
claims.testable: partly - capacity estimates need liquidity data

claims.speaker: Adam Butler
claims.quote: you can model a moving average cross by taking by weighting for example uh longer term moving averages positively and shorter term moving averages negatively
claims.claim: A grid of time-series momentum lookbacks can span continuous moving-average-crossover trend rules (long averages positive, short negative), so a regression on a lookback grid can mimic them; breakout systems with trailing stops and entry-only vol scaling have far more degrees of freedom and are not spanned.
claims.indicator: time-series momentum lookback grid as basis for trend rules
claims.conditions: Applies to continuous trend signals, not event-driven breakouts.
claims.testable: yes - the span can be tested

claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
claims.quote: that comes from what markets are you trading, what trend speeds are you trading, how much risk weight are you giving each market
claims.claim: Dispersion among trend managers comes from implementation choices: which markets, which trend speeds, how much risk weight per market and which constraints; a replication fits all these parameters to the index to remove arbitrary dispersion.
claims.conditions: Cory's 30-second summary of the bottom-up approach.
claims.testable: yes - dispersion attribution to markets, speed and weights

claims.speaker: Moritz (co-host)
claims.quote: with the bottom up approach, you don't necessarily have that response function
claims.claim: A fixed bottom-up fit cannot adapt if the underlying managers change style (for example shifting to faster trends or different markets), unlike a top-down regression, so recalibration frequency is a design question.
claims.conditions: Concern if the index managers' style shifts; Cory answers that annual reruns hardly change the weights.

claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
claims.quote: to deliver the beta of the category and we're trying to outperform that over the long run through feed differentials
claims.claim: The ETF aims to deliver trend beta and beat the category over the long run through lower fees, while managers who want to add alpha should trade the fat tail of markets (which the mutual fund version does).
claims.direction: lower fees give net outperformance of beta
claims.conditions: Valid if the replication tracks the beta closely.
claims.testable: yes - compare ETF net return with the index net of fees

claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
claims.quote: but it's also untethered mechanically from trend following
claims.claim: The top-down regression works but is mechanically untethered from trend following, which is why a mechanistic bottom-up system with almost opposite strengths and weaknesses is added; the two have fairly uncorrelated tracking errors.
claims.conditions: Top-down has no built-in trend rule.
claims.testable: yes - tracking error correlation of the two methods

claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
claims.quote: Our replication approach is truly applying trend following signals. I think a lot of people get that wrong when they talk about replication
claims.claim: Replication is not divorced from trend following: the 70% bottom-up leg applies true trend signals with parameters fitted to the index, and the 30% top-down leg adds process diversification.
claims.conditions: Cory's response to critics of replication.

claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
claims.quote: if they're using faster mean reversion models, it could be very difficult to pick that up
claims.claim: A top-down regression struggles to capture the fast, multi-day mean-reversion models in the broader CTA index because 20-40 daily observations of 20-40 contracts are not enough to fit them, so it ends up capturing mostly the trend part.
claims.indicator: top-down replication of the SG CTA index
claims.direction: trend explains most of the CTA index but the mean-reversion part is missed
claims.conditions: Gets worse as non-trend sleeves grow.
claims.testable: yes - R-squared of CTA index regression on trend only

claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
claims.quote: are just going to get squeezed out by lower cost, more efficient data implementations
claims.claim: Funds charging performance fees for generic trend will be squeezed out by cheaper implementations of the same beta, while fee room remains for managers with real innovation in fat-tail markets, spreads, breakouts and other differentiators.
claims.conditions: Applies to managers whose returns resemble the beta.

claims.speaker: Moritz (co-host)
claims.quote: 10 days ago, we had a little bit of a draw down event, I guess, in the CTA space
claims.claim: As of 15 April 2025 the CTA space had just had a drawdown (equities and trend both falling), and the host hopes it is early innings and that trend recovers within 30-50 days, a reminder that high-stress payoffs arrive with drawdowns first.
claims.conditions: Low-confidence hope, not evidence.

claims.speaker: Adam Butler
claims.quote: we want to have as much allocated to cash uh funded beta where it makes sense, for example, in equities where it's more cash efficient
claims.claim: Stack design: hold equity beta in a cash-funded ETF where that is efficient and top up with S&P futures, while keeping enough cash as collateral for futures strategies, so margin never forces a sale during a drawdown.
claims.conditions: Equities are the most cash-efficient to hold funded.
claims.testable: yes - margin usage can be audited

claims.speaker: Cory Hoffstein
claims.quote: we can do specific short location but we can also get these names on swap
claims.claim: A merger-arbitrage ETF avoids the borrow-fee and recall risk on the short hedge leg of stock-for-stock deals by hedging via swaps as an alternative to physical shorts; most deals are cash, so hedging is rarely needed.
claims.conditions: Applies to stock-for-stock deals.
